stem: A client with diabetes and loss of protective sensation has a thick plantar callus and says, “I’ll trim it myself with a blade and keep wearing my usual tight shoes.” Which response by the nurse is best?

options.A: Avoid self-cutting the callus and arrange appropriate foot-care evaluation; footwear should fit properly and reduce pressure on high-risk areas.
options.B: Trim the callus with a sharp blade after soaking the foot because reduced sensation makes the procedure less painful.
options.C: Continue the tight shoes because pressure on a callus protects the skin underneath from ulceration.
options.D: Ignore the callus unless it becomes painful because loss of protective sensation makes painless lesions low risk.

rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care identify preulcerative corns and calluses, loss of protective sensation, and foot deformity as risk factors for ulceration. ADA preventive guidance advises against self-care of calluses and emphasizes appropriate footwear; people at increased plantar pressure or high risk may need customized pressure-relieving or specialized therapeutic footwear and foot-care specialist involvement. B risks injury to insensate skin. C can increase pressure and tissue damage. D is unsafe because neuropathy can make clinically important injury painless.
educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic loss of protective sensation to avoid self-cutting calluses and use appropriately fitted pressure-reducing footwear with professional foot-care evaluation when risk lesions are present.
source_organization: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee
source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
source_locator: Foot Care — risk factors include LOPS and preulcerative corns/calluses; Recommendation 12.31 therapeutic footwear for high-risk individuals including LOPS/callus; Foot Care Education/Treatment — discuss appropriate footwear and no barefoot walking; initial management includes avoidance of self-care of ingrown nails and calluses and pressure-relieving footwear for increased plantar pressures
source_claim_supported: Loss of protective sensation and callus increase diabetic foot-ulcer risk; clients should avoid self-treatment of calluses and use appropriate footwear/foot-care support to reduce pressure and injury risk.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide preventive teaching for chronic-disease self-care and behaviors that reduce injury and complication risk
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — diabetic callus and footwear self-care teaching
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source broad foot-care list to avoid duplicating V2-Q1445’s daily-inspection construct. The final item focuses on two directly supported high-risk behaviors—avoiding self-cutting of calluses and using appropriate pressure-reducing footwear—and reclassifies the item from Basic Care and Comfort to Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: preventive diabetic foot care / callus and footwear
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 12. ADA identifies callus/LOPS as high-risk features, advises against self-care of calluses, and supports appropriate pressure-relieving or therapeutic footwear when indicated.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A stays within supported preventive actions and does not claim every callus requires the same device or procedure. The stem’s LOPS makes professional evaluation and avoidance of sharp self-treatment clearly appropriate.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it reduces injury and plantar-pressure risk in an insensate foot.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; sharp self-treatment can injure skin when protective sensation is reduced.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; tight footwear can increase pressure and ulcer risk rather than protect the callus.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; painless lesions can still be high risk precisely because neuropathy reduces warning sensation.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A addresses both the unsafe callus treatment and footwear pressure problem.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are concrete foot-care actions responding to the client’s stated plan.
audit_findings.blueprint: Health Promotion and Maintenance is appropriate because the construct centers on preventive self-care education rather than treatment of an established ulcer.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked callus risk, self-care wording, footwear evidence limits, LOPS significance, overlap with Q1445, category mapping, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
